lead: Buoys and lights tell you where the safe water is. In flotilla waters you meet a small set of them: the red and green sides of a channel, the black and yellow cardinals, a few marks that stand alone and the harbour lights.

sections.title: Red to port on the way in

qa.q: Which side do I leave a green buoy on when leaving harbour?
qa.a: To port: in **IALA Region A**, Europe and the Mediterranean, green is left to starboard coming in from sea, and going out everything swaps. Where there is no obvious way in, a chart arrow shows the **direction of buoyage**.

blocks.p: **Lateral marks** show the edges of a channel. They are laid for a boat coming in from the sea. In **IALA Region A**, which covers Europe and the Mediterranean, you leave red marks to port and green marks to starboard on the way in. The shape says the same: a red **can**, a green **cone**.

Going out to sea everything swaps: red stays to starboard, green to port. In a strait between islands there is no "in", so the chart shows the **direction of buoyage** with an arrow, and you treat that direction as coming in. Heading against it, you leave a green cone to port.
**Region B**, the Americas and with them the Caribbean, reverses the colours: coming in, red is left to starboard. The shapes keep their sides: can to port, cone to starboard.

blocks.rule: Region A, coming in from the sea: red to port, green to starboard. Going out: the other way round.

sections.title: Between the red and the green

qa.q: Where do I steer between the red and green harbour lights at night?
qa.a: Between them, keeping **red to port** and green to starboard as you come in. A red light on your starboard bow means you are on the wrong side of it, outside the channel: turn until it is on your port side.

blocks.p: At night the sides keep their colours. Most small harbours show just two lights, a red and a green, one on each pierhead. Coming in, steer between them with the red to port and the green to starboard.

tiles.name: Red on the starboard bow
tiles.note: wrong side: bring it to port

blocks.p: A red light on your starboard bow as you come in means you are on the wrong side of it, outside the channel: turn until it is on your port side. Leaving harbour, the red lights pass down your starboard side.

qa.q: Which side do I pass a west cardinal buoy on?
qa.a: On its west side: a **cardinal mark** is named after the side where the safe water is, so the danger lies east of a west cardinal. At night it shows nine quick white flashes, like nine on a clock face.

blocks.p: A **cardinal mark** stands beside a danger and is named after the side where the safe water is: pass **north of a north** cardinal, east of an east one. The danger lies on the opposite side: a west cardinal has its reef to the east. All four are black and yellow, with two black cones on top.

At night the light is white and counts like a clock face: three quick flashes for east, six for south, nine for west, quick flashes without a break for north. The south cardinal adds one long flash, which sets it apart from three and nine.

Turn the compass side into a side of your boat. Heading east towards a north cardinal, north is to port: turn to port and leave the mark to starboard. Never pass between a north and a south cardinal that guard the same danger.

fig.note: The danger lies between the two marks

blocks.rule: The cones point to the black: up for north, down for south, apart for east, together for west.

qa.q: What does a yellow buoy with an X on top mean?
qa.a: It is a **special mark**: it shows an area, not a danger to steer round. A line of them off a beach is usually the limit of a bathing zone; the chart or pilot book says what they are for.

blocks.p: An **isolated danger mark** sits on a small danger with navigable water all round: black with a red band, two black balls on top. Pass either side, but give it a good berth. A **safe water mark** is the opposite: red and white stripes and a red ball mean deep water all round, often at the start of a fairway.

Yellow **special marks** with an X on top show an area, not a danger to steer round. A line of them off a beach is usually the limit of a bathing zone; the chart or the pilot book tells you what they are for.

sections.title: Reading a light off the chart

qa.q: What does Fl(3) G 10s mean on a chart?
qa.a: A green light flashing in groups of three, the whole pattern repeating every 10 seconds. The **period** is the full cycle, light and dark together; with no colour letter the light would be white.

blocks.p: The chart and the pilot book give every light a short code, so that you can tell it from its neighbours with a watch. **Fl(3) G 10s** reads: flashes in groups of three, green, the whole pattern repeating every 10 seconds. The **period** is the full cycle, light and dark together. No colour letter means a white light.

head: Code
What you see
rows: Flashing: single flashes · groups of two; more dark than light
A long flash, 2 seconds or more
Quick, about one flash a second · very quick, about two

blocks.p: Time a light that is on for 4 seconds and off for 2, and you have Oc 6s. A buoy marked just Q shows white quick flashes without a break: a north cardinal.

A **sector light** shows white over the safe approach and red or green over the dangers to either side. If the white turns to a colour as you come in, you have left the safe sector: check the chart and get back into the white.

tiles.name: White sector
tiles.note: you are on the safe approach

tiles.name: It turns red
tiles.note: off the line: check the chart
